```
contract-guard-starter-kit/
├── README.md

The situation
Acko's services talk to each other through APIs: the mobile app calls the quote service,

service breaks in production. Nobody can say which changes are safe, who uses what, or
who approved a risky change.

The problem
Build Contract Guard: a registry where teams publish each version of their API's
specification. Contract Guard works out exactly what changed between versions,
decides whether each change could break the services that use the API, shows which
services would be affected, and stops dangerous changes from being published without
the right people knowing.
What you get: the starter kit
Unzip it and start it from the kit's folder:
Docker: docker compose up --build
Podman: podman compose up --build
You get:
API specifications for 3 services, quote-api , policy-api  and claims-api , each
with four versions written in OpenAPI 3. Some versions contain problems you'll want
Contract Guard to catch.
Descriptions of 4 services that use these APIs: mobile-app , partner-portal ,
payments-svc  and notifications-svc , in a simple format explained in the kit's
README.
A webhook receiver with a page that shows every notification it receives.
Full details are in the kit's README.

2 Shared components Specifications reuse components through
references ( $ref ). Compare versions on what the
API actually accepts and returns, not on how the
file is organised.

Option 2: Dependency Watch – vulnerability tracking for our 
services
The situation
Every Acko service depends on dozens of open-source packages, and those packages
depend on more packages. Several times a week, a security vulnerability is published for
one of them. Today, finding out which of our services are affected means asking every
team to check by hand. Serious problems get missed, minor ones get the same attention
as critical ones, and nobody knows what's still unfixed or for how long.
The problem
Build Dependency Watch: a service that knows every package each of our services uses,
checks them against a feed of published vulnerabilities, ranks what it finds by real risk,
advises how to fix it, and tracks every finding until it's resolved.
What you get: the starter kit
Unzip it and start it from the kit's folder:
Docker: docker compose up --build
Podman: podman compose up --build
You get:
8 services, each with its dependency files (npm or Python) and a small file describing
the service: its owner, how critical it is, and whether it's reachable from the internet.
A mock vulnerability feed serving advisories in a standard format (OSV). Like a real
feed, it changes: you can switch it to an updated version to see what your product
does when new advisories arrive.
Scripts that change services' dependencies, so you can see what happens when
teams upgrade packages.
A webhook receiver with a page that shows every notification it receives.
Full details are in the kit's README.
Must-haves
These are what a complete product needs. How you build each one is up to you.

# Feature What it means
1 Service inventory Register services with their details. Scan their
dependency files and list every package they use,
including packages pulled in by other packages,
with the version actually in use.
2 Versions and ranges Understand versions and version ranges correctly
for both npm and Python.
3 Vulnerability feed Read advisories from the feed: which package,
which versions are affected, which versions fix it,
and how severe it is. Reading the feed again must
not create duplicates.
4 Matching Find every service affected by every advisory. For a
package pulled in by another package, show the
chain that brings it in.
5 Prioritisation Give every finding a priority, and explain how it was
worked out. Not every finding is equally urgent.
6 Fix advice Say which version fixes the problem, whether the
service can move to it easily, and when the fix
needs a bigger upgrade.
7 Tracking findings Track each finding from when it's found until it's
resolved, with an owner and a due date. Show
what's overdue.
8 Changes over time When the feed or a service's dependencies
change, show what's new, what's resolved and
what's come back.
9 UI Show the biggest risks across all services, each
service's findings, and which services each
vulnerability affects.
10 Metrics and runnable Show how well we're keeping up, for example open

Got it — I've read the PDF. Here's the brief on **Option 1: Contract Guard**.

## What it is (one line)
A registry where API teams publish each version of their OpenAPI spec; the tool figures out exactly what changed between versions, decides which changes would **break the services that call the API**, and **blocks dangerous changes from publishing** without the right people knowing.

## Who it's for
Engineers who own APIs, engineers whose services call them, and platform leads.

## What's expected (the 10 must-haves, grouped)

| Group | What to build |
|---|---|
| **Registry** (1–2) | Register services + owners; upload OpenAPI specs (YAML/JSON) via API + UI; reject invalid specs with clear errors; compare versions by **semantic content** (resolved `$ref`s), not file structure |
| **Diff engine** (3) | Detect every change: endpoints/methods, parameters, request/response fields (nested + lists), types, required flags, enums, status codes |
| **Breaking-change classifier** (4) | For each change: could it break callers? Explain why in plain words. Context matters (e.g. removal vs. addition) |
| **Impact & safety** (5–7) | Consumers register what they send/read; show which services a proposed version affects; **stop publishing** versions that break them |
| **Visibility** (8–9) | Changelog between any two versions, history of every publish attempt; UI showing services, versions, diffs, impact |
| **Ops** (10) | Metrics (e.g. "dangerous changes caught") + starts with one command, runnable from scratch |

**Stretch ideas:** webhook notifications to affected teams, a CI check endpoint, AI-written migration guides.

## The kit you have
3 APIs × 4 versions each (with planted breaking changes), 4 consumer usage files, and a webhook receiver on :9900. Don't modify `specs/` or `consumers/`.

## Timeline & deliverables
- **0:00–1:15** → research, questions to the product owner, design → **PLAN.md (Gate 1)**
- **1:15–3:30** → build → **PROGRESS.md (Gate 2)**
- **3:30–5:30** → build + test (commits every ~45 min)
- **6:00** → README, DECISIONS.md, tests, **transcripts/**, REVIEW.md

## Scoring emphasis (out of 100)
**Design 20 + Building 20 = 40** — a *smaller, working, well-designed product you can explain* beats a bigger broken one. AI usage 15, understanding 12, communication 10, testing 10, planning 8, metrics 5.

**My read:** the heart of this is the **diff engine + breakage classifier** — that's where the design weight sits. A lean product: registry, semantic diff, classifier with explanations, impact check, block-on-publish, one clean UI screen for the diff — is the winning scope.

Yes, your understanding is right — but there are two pieces you're missing that make this product more than a "diff viewer":

## What you've got ✓
- A product with an **interface** (UI + API) where teams register and publish API spec versions
- It tells you **what changed** between two versions
- And **what those changes mean** — if something breaks, it says what the issue is

## What you're missing ✗

**1. It's preventive, not reactive.** The point isn't to diagnose an error *after* something broke in production — it's to catch it **before publishing**. That's why feature #7 exists: publishing a dangerous version is **stopped**. Think of it as a gate/checkpoint, not a debugger. You want to shift the failure from "another team's service crashes at 2am" to "your publish gets blocked with an explanation."

**2. It knows *who* breaks, not just *that* something breaks.** This is the real differentiator. A raw diff tool says "field `premium.total` was removed." Contract Guard says:

> **"Field `premium.total` was removed from the response — this breaks `mobile-app`, which reads that field in `GET /quotes/{id}`."**

That's only possible because consumers **register what they send and read** (the `consumers/` files), and the tool matches changes against that usage.

## Sharpened one-liner
> Contract Guard sits between API providers and their consumers: when a team publishes a new spec version, it computes exactly what changed, matches those changes against what every consuming service actually uses, classifies each change as safe or breaking **with a plain-English reason**, shows the affected teams — and refuses to publish anything that would break them without that being visible.

Want me to open a real pair of spec versions (say `quote-api` v1 → v2) and point out the concrete planted breaking changes? That would make the diff-engine requirements very tangible before you plan.

Command-line tool to compare and detect breaking changes in OpenAPI specs.

Run it locally, in CI via the [GitHub Action](https://github.com/oasdiff/oasdiff-action), or use the hosted PR review workflow at [oasdiff.com](https://www.oasdiff.com) to approve or reject each change with a CI commit status.

## Get started in 30 seconds

[](#get-started-in-30-seconds)

No install needed — try it with Docker against two sample specs:

```
docker run --rm -t tufin/oasdiff changelog \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oasdiff/oasdiff/main/data/openapi-test1.yaml \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oasdiff/oasdiff/main/data/openapi-test5.yaml
```

That prints a human-readable changelog of the changes that can affect API consumers, breaking and non-breaking. Swap `changelog` for `breaking` to see only the changes that break existing API clients, or `diff` for the full machine-readable diff of the API definition, including documentation-only edits.

## Documentation

[](#documentation)

Grouped by what you're trying to do. New to oasdiff? Start with **Commands**.

### Commands

[](#commands)

The top-level subcommands, grouped as in `oasdiff --help`.

**Compare two specs**

- [`breaking`](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/BREAKING-CHANGES.md) — only the changes that break existing API clients

- [`changelog`](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/BREAKING-CHANGES.md) — changes that can affect API consumers, breaking or not, in human-readable form

- [`diff`](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/DIFF.md) — full diff of the API definition, including documentation-only edits (output: html, json, markdown, markup, text, or yaml — default yaml)

- [`summary`](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/DIFF.md) — high-level count of changes between two specs (built on the diff engine; same shared options)

**Process a single spec**

- [`validate`](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/VALIDATE.md) — check a spec for per-RFC violations (invalid types, missing required fields, bad regex, unresolved `$ref`s)

- [`upgrade`](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/OPENAPI-31.md#converting-a-spec-with-oasdiff-upgrade) — canonicalize an OpenAPI 3\.0 spec to the latest 3\.x

- [`flatten`](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/ALLOF.md) — replace `allOf` schemas with a merged equivalent

**Git integration**

- [`breaking-files`](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/BREAKING-FILES.md) — check a list of changed specs against their versions in a git ref, one comparison per spec; used by the [pre-commit hook](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/BREAKING-FILES.md#pre-commit-hook)

- [`git-diff-driver`](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/GIT-DIFF-DRIVER.md) — run as a git external diff driver so `git log --patch` renders an OpenAPI changelog inline

**Reference**

- [`checks changelog`](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/CHECKS.md) — list the rules `breaking` and `changelog` use to classify changes ([customize them](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/CUSTOMIZING-CHECKS.md))

- [`checks validate`](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/CHECKS.md#validate-checks) — list the rules `validate` reports

- [`checks changelog coverage`](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/CHECKS.md#coverage-map) — list every possible edit of an OpenAPI document with the checks that cover it

- [`schema`](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/BREAKING-CHANGES.md#json-schema) — print a JSON Schema for the `breaking`/`changelog` json output

### Inputs

[](#inputs)

Where specs come from.

- [Git revisions](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/GIT-REVISION.md) — compare against a branch, tag, or commit

- Local files, http/s URLs, YAML or JSON — all handled transparently

### Comparison

[](#comparison)

How oasdiff pairs up base and revision and what counts as a difference.

- [Endpoint matching](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/MATCHING-ENDPOINTS.md) — handles renamed path parameters and [duplicate endpoints](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/MATCHING-ENDPOINTS.md#duplicate-endpoints)

- [Nullability changes](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/NULLABILITY.md) — the three equivalent nullable forms and when changing them is breaking

- [Compare APIs split across multiple files](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/COMPOSED.md) — e.g. an API gateway with one spec per service

- [Check many independent specs](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/BREAKING-FILES.md) — one comparison per spec, rather than merging them as composed mode does

- [Filter endpoints](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/FILTERING-ENDPOINTS.md) — narrow the diff to a subset of endpoints

### Normalization

[](#normalization)

Align each spec before diffing so equivalent things line up.

- [Merge `allOf` schemas](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/ALLOF.md)

- [Merge common (path-level) parameters](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/COMMON-PARAMS.md)

- [Path prefix modification](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/PATH-PREFIX.md) — strip or add a prefix so a moved API still matches

- [Case-insensitive header comparison](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/HEADER-DIFF.md) — treat `Content-Type` and `content-type` as the same header

### API lifecycle

[](#api-lifecycle)

Communicate intent across versions.

- [Deprecate APIs and parameters](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/DEPRECATION.md)

- [API stability levels](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/STABILITY.md) (draft / alpha / beta / stable)

- [Version bumps](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/VERSIONING.md) — fail the build when a breaking change is released without a major version bump

### Filtering changes

[](#filtering-changes)

Choose which kinds of differences are reported.

- [Exclude certain kinds of changes](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/DIFF.md#excluding-specific-kinds-of-changes) — e.g. ignore description-only edits

- [Track OpenAPI extensions](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/DIFF.md#openapi-extensions) — opt in to reporting changes in `x-*` fields

- [Exclude specific extension names](/oasdiff/oasdiff/blob/main/docs/DIFF.md#excluding-specific-extension-names) — when extensions are tracked, skip ones you don't care about

API hub provides the **Specification linter** add-on which validates your API's OpenAPI specification. Soon after you add an OpenAPI specification to your API version, the linter validates the specification, and reports the findings in the Google Cloud console. > [!NOTE] > **Note:** The **Specification linter** add-on is enabled by default in API hub. You can disable the linter add-on anytime. See [Disable specification validation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/apihub/validate-spec.md.txt#disable-spec-validation). ## Style guide A style guide is a set of rules against which API hub validates an OpenAPI specification. API hub uses a default style guide for validating the OpenAPI specifications. For the default style guide rules, see [OpenAPI Rules](https://meta.stoplight.io/docs/spectral/4dec24461f3af-open-api-rules). > [!NOTE] > **Note:**To add your own custom rules, you must create a new style guide that extends the default style guide. After adding your custom rules in the new style guide, you must upload the new style guide in API hub. ### Upload a new style guide ### Console To upload a new style guide, do the following steps: 1. Create a new style by extending the default style guide. For more information, see [Create a ruleset](https://meta.stoplight.io/docs/spectral/01baf06bdd05a-create-a-ruleset). 2. In the Google Cloud console, go to the **API hub \> Add-on management** page. 3. Locate the **Specification linter** card, and then click **Manage**. 4. In the **Specification linter** pane, click **Upload new style guide**. 5. Browse to the new style guide that you want to upload, and then click **Open** . The style guide that you selected is uploaded to API hub. 6. Click **Close**. ### REST API To upload a new style guide for linting, issue a `PATCH` request to the following API: `https://apihub.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT/locations/LOCATION/plugins/standard-linter/styleGuide?update_mask=contents` For more information about the API, see [UpdateStyleGuide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/reference/apis/apihub/rest/v1/projects.locations.plugins/updateStyleGuide.md.txt). The following example shows the API call to upload a style guide. ``` curl \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"name":"projects/test-project-1/locations/us-central1/plugins/standard-linter/styleGuide", "contents":{ "contents": "ZXh0ZW5kczogWyJzcGVjdHJhbDpvYXMiXQo=", "mimeType": "text/yaml"}}' \ -X PATCH \ https://apihub.googleapis.com/v1/projects/test-project-1/locations/us-central1/plugins/standard-linter/styleGuide?update_mask=contents ``` ### Download the default style guide To download the default style guide used by API hub for linting, do the following steps: 1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the **API hub \> Add-on management** page. 2. Locate the **Specification linter** card, and then click **Manage**. 3. In the **Specification linter** pane, click **Download default style guide**. 4. Click **Close**. ### Download the latest style guide ### Console To download the style guide that is currently used by API hub for linting, do the following steps: 1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the **API hub \> Add-on management** page. 2. Locate the **Specification linter** card, and then click **Manage**. 3. In the **Specification linter** pane, click **Download latest style guide**. 4. Click **Close**. ### REST API To download the style guide that is currently used by API hub for linting, issue a `GET` request to the following API: `https://apihub.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT/locations/LOCATION/plugins/standard-linter/styleGuide:contents` For more information about the API, see [GetStyleGuide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/reference/apis/apihub/rest/v1/projects.locations.plugins/getStyleGuide.md.txt). The following example shows the API call to download the current style guide. ``` curl -X \ GET -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token)" \ https://apihub.googleapis.com/v1/projects/test-project-1/locations/us-central1/plugins/standard-linter/styleGuide:contents ``` ## Disable specification linter By default, the **Specification linter** add-on is enabled in API hub. If you don't want to validate your API specifications, you can disable the linter add-on. To disable the linter add-on, do the following steps: 1. In the Google Cloud console, go to the **API hub \> Add-on management** page. [Go to Add-on management](https://console.cloud.google.com/apigee/api-hub/add-on-management) 2. Locate the **Specification linter** card and click **Manage** . The **Specification linter** pane appears. To disable the add-on, click **Disable specification linter** , and then click **Disable** in the confirmation dialog.
3. Click **Save**. ### Limitations The following limitations apply when creating and uploading custom style guides: - **No URLs in `extends` property** : Style guides can't contain URLs. Ensure that you don't include any URLs in the `extends` property of your ruleset when creating and uploading a style guide. For example, the following property construction might cause the upload to fail: `extends: [spectral:oas", "https://mystyle.com/"]`. - **`functionsDir` not allowed** : The `functionsDir` property is not allowed in custom style guides. Spectral style guides with JavaScript will not be executed by API hub during the linting process. As a workaround, if you require the use of a custom style guide with JavaScript functions, perform the following steps: 1. Run [Spectral](https://stoplight.io/open-source/spectral) outside of API hub using your custom style guide. 2. Update the linting results in the `Lint` attribute of the specification file in API hub.

## Phase 1 — Discovery: Contract Guard

**No project files have been changed.** I reviewed the problem statement and starter kit, including its consumer declarations, webhook receiver, and the three APIs’ versioned specs.

### Problem and users

Contract Guard aims to prevent an API provider’s change from unexpectedly breaking services that consume that API. Before a new spec version is published, the product should explain what changed, identify which registered consumers may be affected, and prevent a risky publish.

The problem statement identifies these users:

- **API-owning engineers:** publish versions and understand the consequences of changes.
- **Consumer engineers:** see whether their service is affected and why.
- **Platform leads:** oversee API changes, publishing outcomes, and protection metrics.

The primary outcome is **catching and explaining consumer-impacting changes before release**, rather than diagnosing production failures afterward.

### Requirements stated in the problem

The product must:

1. Register services and owners.
2. Accept OpenAPI YAML or JSON through both a UI and API; reject invalid specs with clear errors.
3. Compare the API’s meaning across versions, including resolving shared `$ref` components rather than treating file reorganization as a change.
4. Detect changes to operations, parameters, request/response fields (including nested and list fields), types, requiredness, allowed values, and response codes.
5. Classify changes as potentially breaking and explain why in plain language.
6. Register consumers’ API usage and show which consumers are affected by a proposed version and which changes affect them.
7. Block publishing a version that would break consumers.
8. Keep readable changelogs and a history of publish attempts and outcomes.
9. Provide a UI for services, versions, changes, and impact.
10. Include protection metrics and run from one command with setup instructions.

**Explicit stretch items:** webhook notifications, a CI check endpoint, and AI-generated migration guidance. They are optional, not core requirements.

### What the starter kit provides

- Three providers — `quote-api`, `policy-api`, `claims-api` — with four spec files each.
- Four consumer YAML files describing endpoints and fields each consumer sends or reads.
- A webhook receiver that accepts POST requests and displays notifications.
- A rule not to modify the supplied `specs/` or `consumers/` files.

The README leaves it to the product to decide whether to import those files, upload their contents, or support both.

### Concrete cases to account for

These examples come from the supplied files; they are useful acceptance-test scenarios:

- **Quote API:** the response field `premium.breakdown[].amount` becomes `value`. `mobile-app` reads `amount`, so it should be identified as affected. The GET route placeholder also changes from `{id}` to `{quoteId}`; the impact policy for placeholder renames needs clarification.
- **Policy API:** `legacyCode` is deprecated and later removed; `payments-svc` reads it. `phone` is also deprecated and later removed, though the supplied consumer declarations do not show it being read. The final endorsement spec makes `requestedBy` required and removes `VEHICLE` from allowed `type` values; `partner-portal` sends `type` and does not declare `requestedBy`.
- **Claims API:** one version contains an unresolved `$ref` (`ClaimDocumnt`), which should be rejected as invalid with a useful error. The later version fixes it. The final version makes `amountApproved` optional while `mobile-app` reads it, which may make the value absent at runtime.

The kit also has details worth clarifying: the claims files numbered 2 and 3 both declare `info.version: 1.1.0`, and the policy API’s `x-sunset` date for `legacyCode` is `2026-11-01`, which is in the past relative to today. These make version-ordering and sunset behavior concrete requirements to resolve, not just implementation details.

### Non-functional requirements and assumptions

**Explicit:** clear validation errors; one-command runnable setup; readable history/changelog; a product small enough to test and explain.

**Not specified:** authentication/authorization, concurrent publishing, database choice, deployment environment, performance targets, data retention, upload limits, or production security. For a local buildathon product, a local single-user workflow and lightweight persistence may be sensible, but those are assumptions to confirm rather than stated requirements.

### Ambiguities and edge cases

The main product decisions still open are:

- Does *any* potentially breaking change block publishing, or only a change that impacts a **declared** consumer?
- Are unregistered consumers considered? How do we avoid presenting “no known impact” as proof that a change is safe?
- Are changes classified globally, or does the answer depend on direction and context? For example, adding a response enum value can break strict clients, while adding an optional request field is usually compatible.
- Is a deprecated field allowed to remain publishable until its sunset date? What happens after that date, and what exactly does `x-sunset` mean?
- Does “owner approval” mean a formal approval workflow, or does the product only need to show/block changes? The statement mentions the right people knowing, but doesn’t specify roles or approval steps.
- Are duplicate `info.version` values valid when file order indicates separate versions?
- Should route-parameter placeholder renames be treated as breaking, given the actual URL shape may remain the same but generated client method signatures may change?
- How should the system handle unsupported OpenAPI constructs, external `$ref`s, multiple media types, and cyclic references?

### Questions to ask the product owner

1. What precisely do `x-internal` and `x-sunset` mean, and should internal operations be excluded from consumer impact?
2. What severity categories should the product use, and which categories block publish?
3. Should publish be blocked only when a declared consumer is affected, or also for breaking changes with unknown consumers?
4. Can an owner override a block? If yes, should the product record a reason or approval?
5. Should versions be ordered by filename/import order, `info.version`, or an explicit user selection? How should duplicate version strings be handled?
6. Does deprecation warn only, or does it affect publish decisions? How should a past sunset date be handled?
7. What is the expected consumer onboarding path: import the kit’s files, manual UI entry, API registration, or all three?
8. Are notifications or a CI endpoint important enough to prioritize after core must-haves?

### Comparable products — researched facts

- **oasdiff** documents separate commands for a full API diff, a human-readable changelog, and breaking-change reporting. Its documentation also describes spec validation and handling of `$ref`/normalization concerns. This suggests keeping validation, semantic comparison, and breaking-change classification as distinct capabilities. [oasdiff](https://github.com/oasdiff/oasdiff)
- **Google Apigee API hub** documents OpenAPI specification linting with a default style guide and support for custom rules. That is adjacent to Contract Guard’s validation and governance needs, though it is not evidence that the same policy choices are required here. [Apigee specification validation](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/apihub/validate-spec)

These are product/documentation observations, not recommendations to adopt either product or dependency.

**Phase 1 is complete.** The key unresolved decisions are the blocking policy, consumer-unknown behavior, approval/override expectations, and how to interpret `x-internal`/`x-sunset`. The next phase is design; per your workflow, I’ll wait for your direction before drafting `PLAN.md` or proposing a finalized architecture.

Understood. I’ll use your answers as working decisions and define the core design **up to the two pending product-owner answers**. I won’t create or edit `PLAN.md` yet; this is the design proposal for you to review first.

## Agreed decisions

- **Consumer impact:** assess only consumers registered in the supplied declarations. The result should say “no declared consumer affected,” not imply that no other consumers exist.
- **Version ordering:** use the OpenAPI `info.version` values to identify and compare versions. Warn on duplicates.
- **Duplicate versions:** I recommend **not overwriting a published version**, even with confirmation, because that would erase history and make changelogs and audit records unreliable. Instead, let the user import it under a different version, or replace it only while it is still an unpublished draft. Please confirm if you specifically want published versions to be overwritable.
- **Starter-kit data:** import the supplied specs and consumer declarations for the initial experience. Also provide spec upload through the UI and API, since both are explicit requirements. The import is a convenient bootstrap path, not a replacement for those upload capabilities.
- **Scope:** focus on the required registry, validation, comparison, consumer impact, safe publishing, history, UI, and metrics. Defer notifications, CI integration, and AI-generated guidance.
- **Tech:** Python/FastAPI backend, React frontend, PostgreSQL if persistence is used.

## Suggested core product structure

**Frontend (React):**
1. **Services** — providers, owners, and available versions.
2. **Service detail** — upload/import a spec; view versions and validation status.
3. **Compare versions** — select a baseline and proposed version; inspect changes and explanations.
4. **Impact and publish** — affected declared consumers, relevant changes, and publish outcome.
5. **History and metrics** — publish attempts, outcomes, and counts of detected/blocked risky changes.

**Backend (FastAPI):**
- **Registry:** services, owners, versions, consumer records.
- **Spec validation:** parse YAML/JSON and validate OpenAPI structure and internal `$ref`s; return actionable errors.
- **Comparison:** compare normalized API meaning, so moving a schema into or out of `components` alone is not reported as an API change.
- **Classification and impact:** classify changes, match them to each declared consumer’s endpoint and `sends`/`reads`, and explain the match.
- **Publishing:** record each attempt and its result; apply the agreed block policy once the owner answers.
- **Import/API routes:** bootstrap the starter-kit files and support spec upload and consumer registration.

These should be separate modules in one application rather than separate services; that keeps the build simpler to implement and run.

## Initial data model

A compact relational model should cover:

- **Service:** name, type (provider or consumer), owner/team.
- **SpecVersion:** provider service, `info.version`, original document, normalized representation, validation result, creation time, and status.
- **ConsumerUsage:** consumer service, provider service, method, path, sent paths, read paths.
- **PublishAttempt:** proposed version, baseline version, outcome, timestamp, and reason.
- **ChangeFinding:** comparison, change type, API location, before/after details, classification, explanation, and affected consumers.

Keeping original spec contents and each publish attempt supports traceability. Published versions should be immutable under the recommendation above.

## API shape (proposal)

- `GET /api/services` — list registered services.
- `GET /api/services/{id}/versions` — list versions for a provider.
- `POST /api/services/{id}/versions` — upload and validate YAML/JSON.
- `POST /api/import/starter-kit` — import the supplied specs and consumer declarations.
- `GET /api/versions/{from_id}/compare/{to_id}` — return changes, classifications, and consumer impact.
- `POST /api/versions/{id}/publish` — record an attempt and publish or block it according to policy.
- `GET /api/publish-attempts` and `GET /api/metrics` — history and summary metrics.

These are draft contracts, not settled implementation details.

## Two decisions still needed

1. **Severity and blocking:** which severity levels should findings use, and which levels block publishing? I can still design findings and impact reporting now, but the final publish gate depends on this answer.
2. **Deprecation and sunset behavior:** should `deprecated`/`x-sunset` only warn, or affect publishing—and, if they do, when? This affects the policy rules, not whether we parse and display those extensions.

## One suggestion on importing vs registration

Importing is the quickest way to get meaningful comparisons from the supplied exercise data. I suggest importing **both the specs and consumer declarations**, showing a clear summary and any validation failures. For subsequent use, spec upload through UI/API and consumer registration/editing should still be available. That meets the stated requirements without making starter-kit import the only way to use the product.

Once you confirm the overwrite recommendation and the owner answers questions 2 and 6, I can finalize the design and prepare the plan for your approval before implementation.

# Phase 2 — Proposed design

I’ll treat the following as the provisional product policy until the product owner says otherwise:

- **Breaking change:** block publishing only if it impacts a **declared consumer**.
- **Deprecated or sunset element:** warn before its `x-sunset` date; after that date, block publishing if a declared consumer still uses the element.
- Keep these rules separate from comparison and impact analysis, so they can be changed later without rewriting those parts.

For date handling, my proposed assumption is that an element is expired once its `x-sunset` calendar date has passed. If the product owner specifies different date semantics, that can be changed in the policy configuration.

## Architecture

Use a **single FastAPI application**, a **React UI**, and **PostgreSQL**. PostgreSQL is justified because the product needs durable versions, consumer declarations, publish attempts, and history. Keep the backend modular rather than splitting it into services:

1. **Registry and import** — services, owners, spec versions, consumer usage, and starter-kit import.
2. **Validation** — parse YAML/JSON, validate OpenAPI, and report clear errors, including unresolved local `$ref`s.
3. **Comparison** — compare API meaning after resolving local `$ref`s, so reorganizing components alone is not shown as an API change.
4. **Classification and impact** — interpret each change in context, match it against declared consumer usage, and explain the result.
5. **Publish policy** — apply configurable rules to the findings and decide whether to publish or block.
6. **History and metrics** — retain publish outcomes and provide summary counts.

Use the existing webhook receiver unchanged. Notifications are optional, so the core product does not need to send webhooks initially.

## Main workflow

1. Import the starter-kit specs and consumer declarations.
2. Select a provider and upload a proposed OpenAPI YAML or JSON spec.
3. Validate the spec; reject invalid input with a useful error.
4. Compare it to a selected existing version.
5. Show changes, their classifications, and any affected declared consumers.
6. Apply the publish policy and record the attempt as **published** or **blocked**, with a reason.
7. Keep the comparison and outcome available in the service’s history.

A provider can also upload specs and register consumers through the UI and API; starter-kit import is a bootstrap path, not the only way to use the product.

## Core data model

- **Service** — name, provider/consumer role, owner/team.
- **SpecVersion** — provider, `info.version`, spec content, validation status, timestamps.
- **SpecRevision** — immutable content revision for a version number. If an import finds a duplicate version, warn and allow an explicit overwrite; preserve the previous content as a revision so published history and previous comparisons remain auditable.
- **ConsumerUsage** — consumer, provider, method, path, and the declared `sends` and `reads` paths.
- **PublishAttempt** — proposed revision, baseline, outcome, timestamp, and policy reason.
- **ChangeFinding** — change category and API location, before/after details, classification, explanation, and affected consumers.

## API outline

- `GET /api/services` — list services.
- `GET /api/services/{service_id}/versions` — list provider versions.
- `POST /api/services/{service_id}/versions` — upload and validate a spec.
- `POST /api/import/starter-kit` — import supplied specs and consumer declarations.
- `GET /api/versions/{from_id}/compare/{to_id}` — return changes, explanations, and consumer impact.
- `POST /api/versions/{version_id}/publish` — record the attempt and publish or block according to policy.
- `GET /api/publish-attempts` — list publish history.
- `GET /api/metrics` — return protection metrics.

These are design-level routes; request and response details can be finalized when implementation begins.

## Change classification and impact

The classifier should consider whether a changed element is in a **request** or a **response**, and whether the consumer declares it under `sends` or `reads`. For example, removing a response field that a consumer reads is a likely break; making a request field required can break consumers that do not send it. Each finding should identify the API location, explain the compatibility concern in plain language, and name the affected consumer where there is a match.

Matching should account for nested fields and list paths such as `premium.breakdown[].amount`. It should also normalize path parameter names when matching endpoint shapes, while reporting route changes in the diff.

For the supplied extensions, `x-internal` marks an element as internal and `x-sunset` indicates its end-of-life date. Their exact effect on publishing will live in the policy rules, not be baked into the diff engine.

## Main screens

1. **Services** — providers and consumers, owners, and available spec versions.
2. **Service detail** — upload/import, validation outcome, and version history.
3. **Compare** — baseline and proposed version, grouped changes, classification, and explanations.
4. **Impact and publish** — affected declared consumers, relevant findings, and a clear publish/block result.
5. **History and metrics** — prior attempts and summary protection measures.

## Test strategy

- **Unit:** spec validation, `$ref` resolution, comparison, change classification, consumer path matching, and policy decisions (including pre-/post-sunset behavior).
- **Integration:** FastAPI upload/import/compare/publish flows against PostgreSQL; verify attempts and revisions persist.
- **Acceptance:** import the supplied kit, compare its versions, check known consumer impacts, reject the invalid Claims spec with a useful error, and verify a blocked publish leaves history intact.
- **UI:** cover the primary path from selecting a service through reviewing impact and seeing the publish outcome.

I won’t describe tests as passing until they are actually run.

## Success metrics

The product should be able to report:

- Number of publish attempts and outcomes.
- Number of publishes blocked due to declared consumer impact.
- Number of affected declared consumers identified.
- Number of expired, consumer-used elements that triggered a block.
- Number of invalid specs rejected.

These are initial operational measures; they do not prove that every real consumer has been registered.

## Build order

1. Import and registry, including useful validation errors.
2. Semantic comparison and readable change findings.
3. Consumer impact matching.
4. Configurable publish policy and attempt history.
5. React screens, metrics, tests, and runnable setup.

This order builds the required flow without taking on optional notifications or CI integration first.

**Design review needed:** please approve this direction or tell me what to adjust. I have not created or changed project files. Once you approve, I can prepare the required `PLAN.md`; implementation remains a separate later phase.

content.text:
# Revised Phase 2 design — Contract Guard

**No files have been changed.** This revision replaces the earlier overwrite proposal: Contract Guard will never silently overwrite an existing spec version. It will detect version collisions, warn the user, and preserve the existing record and history.

## Decisions and provisional policy

- Compare and block changes based on the **declared consumers** only. Say “no declared consumer affected,” not “no consumers affected.”
- Use the OpenAPI `info.version` value as the version identifier.
- If an uploaded spec’s version overlaps an existing version **for that provider**, show a clear warning and do not overwrite. The user can resolve it by changing the proposed version and uploading again, or canceling the upload.
- Keep published versions immutable. Record each publish attempt and its outcome.
- A change classified as breaking blocks publishing only when it impacts a declared consumer.
- A deprecated or sunset element warns before its sunset date. Once `x-sunset` has passed, block publishing if a declared consumer still uses that element.
- Keep classification and publish policy separate, so the product owner’s rules can be adjusted without rewriting validation, comparison, or impact matching.
- Treat `x-internal` as an OpenAPI extension marking internal use, and `x-sunset` as its end-of-life date. Neither extension is required to be present.

The owner’s answers on severity and deprecation/sunset rules are still pending. These are working defaults until those answers arrive.

## Version-collision behavior

When the same provider already has a record with the proposed `info.version`, the UI should:

1. Identify the conflicting version and show its existing status.
2. Explain that replacing it is not allowed because it could erase history or change prior comparisons.
3. Offer **cancel** or **upload a corrected spec with a different version**.
4. Preserve the existing spec and all recorded comparisons and publish attempts.

The collision is scoped to one provider; two different providers may use the same version string. Do not merge records just because they share a version or have identical content.

**Starter-kit edge case:** the two middle Claims API specs both declare `info.version: 1.1.0`. Import must preserve both supplied files and warn rather than overwrite either. Since version numbers alone cannot order two identical version strings, display them distinctly using their source filenames, allow explicit comparison between selected records, and require the version conflict to be resolved before either can be published as a new unique version. Do not change the starter-kit files.

## Architecture

Build one maintainable application, not a distributed system:

- **Backend:** FastAPI, organized into registry/import, validation, comparison, impact/classification, publish-policy, and history/metrics modules.
- **Frontend:** React screens for services, versions, comparison, impact/publishing, and history/metrics.
- **Database:** PostgreSQL for durable service records, uploaded specs, consumer declarations, findings, and publish attempts.
- **Starter kit:** import the original spec and consumer files; leave the kit’s `specs/` and `consumers/` unchanged. Also support spec uploads through the UI and API, as required.
- **Webhook receiver:** reuse the provided receiver unchanged if notifications are added later. Notifications are out of core scope.

## Core workflow

1. Import the starter-kit specs and consumer declarations.
2. Register or select a provider; upload an OpenAPI YAML or JSON spec.
3. Validate it, including checking local `$ref`s; return a clear error if invalid.
4. Check whether its provider and `info.version` collide with an existing record. Warn and preserve the existing record—never overwrite.
5. Compare the proposed spec with a selected baseline, resolving shared components so file reorganization alone is not reported as an API change.
6. Show each change, its classification and explanation, and any affected declared consumers.
7. Apply the configurable policy. Publish or block with a recorded reason.
8. Retain the spec, comparison findings, and attempt outcome in history.

## Data model

- **Service:** name, provider/consumer role, owner/team.
- **SpecVersion:** provider service, `info.version`, original uploaded document, validation result, status, source filename (useful for imports), and timestamps.
- **ConsumerUsage:** consumer service, provider service, method, path, and declared `sends` and `reads` paths.
- **ChangeFinding:** comparison, API location and change type, before/after details, classification, plain-language explanation, and affected consumers.
- **PublishAttempt:** proposed spec record, selected baseline, outcome, timestamp, and policy reason.

Enforce provider-scoped version collision detection. A collision must not replace the existing record. Preserve uploaded spec content and publish history so results remain auditable.

## API outline

- `GET /api/services` — list services and owners.
- `GET /api/services/{service_id}/versions` — list specs and statuses for a provider.
- `POST /api/services/{service_id}/versions` — upload and validate a spec; return validation errors or a version-collision warning without overwriting.
- `POST /api/import/starter-kit` — import supplied specs and consumers while reporting conflicts.
- `GET /api/versions/{from_id}/compare/{to_id}` — compare two selected spec records and return changes, explanations, and impact.
- `POST /api/versions/{version_id}/publish` — record an attempt and publish or block based on policy.
- `GET /api/publish-attempts` — list outcomes and reasons.
- `GET /api/metrics` — return protection metrics.

Exact payload schemas can be specified when implementation is approved.

## Classification and impact

Compare endpoints, methods, parameters, request/response schemas, nested and list fields, types, requiredness, allowed values, and response status codes. Resolve local `$ref`s before comparing so an equivalent reorganization is not reported as a contract change.

Match changes to the consumer’s declared provider, method, path, and `sends`/`reads` paths. For example, removing a response field a consumer reads is a potential break; making a request field required may break a consumer that does not declare sending it. Match nested/list paths such as `premium.breakdown[].amount`.

Each finding should explain:

- What changed and where.
- Whether it is potentially breaking or a deprecation/sunset concern.
- Which declared consumer is affected and how.
- Whether the current publish policy blocks the proposed version.

## Main screens

1. **Services:** provider and consumer services, owners, and spec-version status.
2. **Service detail:** versions, import/upload actions, validation results, and collision warnings.
3. **Compare:** select two spec records; view grouped changes and plain-language explanations.
4. **Impact and publish:** affected declared consumers, policy result, and publish/block action.
5. **History and metrics:** prior attempts, reasons, and summary counts.

## Test strategy

content.text:
Yes. The cleanest approach is to **separate a spec record’s identity from its OpenAPI version number**. That lets the starter kit import intact, keeps the two Claims `1.1.0` files available for comparison, and prevents new uploads from accidentally replacing or ambiguously duplicating a version.

## Revised version and import rules

- Every spec record gets its own internal ID; its OpenAPI `info.version` remains unchanged.
- During starter-kit import, **import every file**, even when a provider has duplicate `info.version` values. Show a warning and distinguish the records by source filename, e.g. `1.1.0 — 2-channel-and-notes` and `1.1.0 — 3-channel-and-notes-fixed`.
- Preserve the original file, record, and comparison history. Never overwrite an existing record.
- Let users compare explicitly selected records, even when their version strings match.
- For a **new UI/API upload**, reject a duplicate provider + `info.version` and explain how to resolve it. The user can cancel or upload a corrected spec with a new version.
- Don’t invent or modify version numbers during import. The imported specs are reference history; a newly proposed release must have a unique version.

This handles the supplied duplicate without breaking import, while keeping future publishing unambiguous.

## Design changes

In the data model, `SpecVersion` should use an internal ID as its primary identity and store `info.version` and `source_filename` separately. Duplicate strings are allowed for imported records but not for new uploads. Publish attempts refer to internal record IDs, so the system always knows exactly which spec was compared or published.

The import flow should **report conflicts as warnings, not fail the entire import**. For normal uploads, a version collision should stop that upload before it replaces anything. The comparison UI should show both the version string and source filename where needed.

This replaces the earlier idea of resolving imported duplicates before they can be used: the two supplied Claims records remain usable for import and comparison, but new uploads still require unique version numbers. No files have been changed; the design remains awaiting your approval.

+# Contract Guard — Gate 1 Plan

+## Problem and users
+
+Contract Guard is a registry and publishing gate for OpenAPI services. It helps API owners understand whether a proposed spec change affects known consumers before publishing; consumer teams can see what changed and why it may affect them; platform leads can review outcomes and protection metrics.
+
+The desired outcome is to catch and explain consumer-impacting API changes before release, not to debug production failures afterward. Impact analysis is explicitly limited to declared consumers; the UI must say “no declared consumer affected,” not claim that there are no other consumers.
+
+## Requirements
+
+### Explicit must-haves
+
+- Register services and owners.
+- Upload OpenAPI YAML or JSON through UI and API; reject invalid specifications with clear errors.
+- Compare versions semantically, resolving shared components and `$ref`s so file organization changes alone are not reported as API changes.
+- Detect changes to operations, methods, parameters, nested/list request and response fields, types, requiredness, allowed values, and response status codes.
+- Classify changes and explain potential breakage in plain language.
+- Register consumer usage and show affected consumers and relevant changes.
+- Block publishing changes that break declared consumers.
+- Show readable changelogs and publish-attempt history.
+- Provide a UI, useful protection metrics, and one-command startup with setup documentation.
+
+### Agreed provisional policy
+
+- A breaking change blocks publishing only if it impacts a declared consumer.
+- A deprecated or `x-sunset` element warns before its sunset date. After the date has passed, block publishing if a declared consumer still uses the element.
+- Keep classification and publish-policy decisions separate/configurable so the product owner can change policy later.
+- Treat `x-internal` as an OpenAPI extension indicating internal use and `x-sunset` as an end-of-life date. Neither extension is required in a spec.
+- Owner answers on severity and sunset/deprecation policy are pending; these are defaults until clarified.
+
+## Starter kit and import decisions
+
+- Import all three providers’ four spec files and all four consumer declarations. Do not modify the supplied `specs/` or `consumers/` files.
+- Support normal spec uploads through UI and API in addition to starter-kit import.
+- Preserve every imported file, including the two Claims specs both declaring `info.version: 1.1.0`.
+- Give each spec record an internal ID. Store `info.version` and source filename separately; use filename to distinguish same-version imported records.
+- Allow duplicate version strings in starter-kit imports with a warning, without failing the entire import. Allow explicit comparison of selected records even when their `info.version` strings match.
+- For new uploads, reject a duplicate provider + `info.version` before overwriting anything; explain that the user should cancel or upload a corrected spec with a unique version. Never overwrite an existing record or its history.
+- Compare explicit spec records; do not infer ordering between duplicate version strings or alter version strings during import.
+
+## Discovery questions and answers
+
+- `x-internal`/`x-sunset` meaning: treat the former as marking internal use and the latter as end-of-life date; neither is mandatory.

+- How to order/identify specs? Use `info.version`; internal record IDs distinguish records. Warn on duplicate imported versions; reject new upload collisions rather than overwrite.

+

+
+Report tests as passing only after actually executing them.
+

+- Publishes blocked due to a declared-consumer break.
+- Declared consumers identified as affected.
+- Blocks due to expired elements still used by declared consumers.
+- Invalid specs rejected.
+- Duplicate version collisions detected without overwriting records.
+
+Metrics describe only loaded/declared data; they do not prove no undeclared consumers exist.
+

+

+

+Product owner still needs to specify severity levels and exact deprecation/sunset behavior. Keep these in policy configuration and update this plan/decision log when answers arrive. Also confirm the default date-boundary meaning of `x-sunset` if the owner has a preference.

55: ## Scope and priorities
56: 
57: ### Build first
58: 
59: 1. Registry, starter-kit import, YAML/JSON validation, local `$ref` checks, useful validation/collision messages.
60: 2. Semantic OpenAPI comparison and human-readable findings.
61: 3. Consumer matching for methods, endpoint shapes, sent/read paths, nested fields, and list paths.
62: 4. Configurable publishing policy, publish outcomes, and immutable/auditable history.
63: 5. React UI, metrics, tests, and one-command runnable setup.
64: 
65: ### Defer
66: 
67: - Webhook notifications, CI check endpoint, AI-generated migration guides, authentication/authorization, distributed deployment, and production-scale performance work unless later required by the product owner.
68: 
69: ## System design
70: 
71: Use one modular application to keep the buildathon product understandable and easy to run:
72: 
73: - **Backend:** Python FastAPI modules for registry/import, validation, comparison, impact/classification, publishing policy, history, and metrics.
74: - **Frontend:** React UI for services, versions, upload/import, comparison, impact/publish, and history/metrics.
75: - **Persistence:** PostgreSQL for service records, spec documents/metadata, consumer declarations, findings, and attempts.
76: - **Starter kit:** import original files without changing them. Reuse the webhook receiver unchanged only if notifications are added later.
77: 
78: ### Data model
79: 
80: - `Service`: name, provider/consumer role, owner/team.
81: - `SpecVersion`: internal ID, provider service, OpenAPI `info.version`, original document, source filename, validation result, status, timestamps.
82: - `ConsumerUsage`: consumer, provider, method, path, `sends`, and `reads` field paths.
83: - `ChangeFinding`: comparison, change kind/location, before/after values, classification, explanation, affected declared consumers.
84: - `PublishAttempt`: proposed spec record, selected baseline, outcome, timestamp, and policy reason.
85: 
86: Enforce provider-scoped unique `info.version` for new UI/API uploads. Starter-kit import may retain duplicate version strings, distinguished by internal ID and filename. Never overwrite existing records. Publish attempts point to record IDs, preserving exact provenance.
87: 
88: ### API outline
89: 
90: - `GET /api/services` — services and owners.
91: - `GET /api/services/{service_id}/versions` — spec records and statuses.
92: - `POST /api/services/{service_id}/versions` — upload and validate; collision returns a warning/error without overwriting.
93: - `POST /api/import/starter-kit` — import specs and consumer declarations; report duplicate-version warnings while preserving every file.
94: - `GET /api/versions/{from_id}/compare/{to_id}` — changes, explanations, and impact for explicitly selected spec records.
95: - `POST /api/versions/{version_id}/publish` — record publish attempt and publish/block per configurable policy.
96: - `GET /api/publish-attempts` — outcomes and reasons.
97: - `GET /api/metrics` — protection summary.
98: 
99: Exact payload contracts can be finalized during implementation design.
100: 
101: ## Main screens
102: 
103: 1. **Services:** provider/consumer list, owners, version counts/status.
104: 2. **Service detail:** version records, source filename, upload/import, validation result, duplicate-version warning.
105: 3. **Compare:** choose exact baseline/proposed records; display semantic changes grouped by operation/schema with before/after and plain-language explanation.
106: 4. **Impact and publish:** affected declared consumers, policy outcome, and publish/block action.
107: 5. **History and metrics:** attempts, reasons, blocked/published counts, affected consumers, expired used elements, invalid specs, and detected version collisions.
108: 
109: ## Test strategy
110: 
111: - **Unit:** YAML/JSON parsing, OpenAPI validation, local `$ref` resolution/errors, normalization, diff categories, classification by request/response direction, consumer nested/list-path matching, duplicate-version rules, and policy boundaries before/on/after sunset.
112: - **Integration:** import/upload/compare/publish against PostgreSQL; confirm all starter files persist, imported duplicate versions warn without loss, new-upload collision does not overwrite, and attempts/findings remain traceable.
113: - **Acceptance:** import full kit; inspect duplicate Claims `1.1.0` entries; reject the Claims spec with unresolved `$ref` and a useful message; demonstrate known quote/policy/claims consumer impacts; verify policy blocks and allowed publishes; review history/metrics.
114: - **UI:** exercise import, upload, collision warning, compare, impact review, publish outcome, and history.
115: 
116: Report tests as passing only after actually executing them.
117: 
118: ## Success metrics
119: 
120: - Publish attempts by outcome.
121: - Publishes blocked due to a declared-consumer break.
122: - Declared consumers identified as affected.
123: - Blocks due to expired elements still used by declared consumers.
124: - Invalid specs rejected.
125: - Duplicate version collisions detected without overwriting records.
126: 
127: Metrics describe only loaded/declared data; they do not prove no undeclared consumers exist.
128: 
129: ## Known edge cases
130: 
131: - Two Claims starter-kit files declare `info.version: 1.1.0`; import both, distinguish by source filename and internal ID, warn, and allow explicitly selected comparison.
132: - A Claims spec has an unresolved local `$ref`; reject it for upload with a precise error, while import should report the invalid record clearly and continue importing other files.
133: - A deprecated/sunset field may be consumer-used; policy depends on the sunset date and must be timezone/date-boundary tested.
134: - Path placeholder names may change while endpoint shape stays similar; compare routes semantically for consumer matching but report route changes to users.
135: - Consumers describe what they used when written; do not assume declarations are current or exhaustive.
136: 
137: ## Pending decisions
138: 
139: Product owner still needs to specify severity levels and exact deprecation/sunset behavior. Keep these in policy configuration and update this plan/decision log when answers arrive. Also confirm the default date-boundary meaning of `x-sunset` if the owner has a preference.

+# Contract Guard — Build Plan
+
+## Problem and users
+
+Contract Guard helps API-owning engineers understand and prevent changes that break known consumers before publishing. Consumer engineers need clear impact and reasons; platform leads need visibility into publishing outcomes. Impact is limited to registered consumer declarations, so reports must say “no declared consumer affected” rather than claim there are no consumers.
+
+## Requirements and decisions

+import json
+from typing import Any, Dict, List, Tuple

+class SpecError(ValueError):

+def parse_document(raw: str, filename: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
+    try:
+        parsed = json.loads(raw) if filename.lower().endswith(".json") else yaml.safe_load(raw)
+    except (ValueError, yaml.YAMLError) as exc:
+        raise SpecError("Could not parse specification: {}".format(exc))
+    if not isinstance(parsed, dict):
+        raise SpecError("Specification root must be an object.")
+    return parsed
+
+
+def validate_document(document: Dict[str, Any]) -> List[str]:
+    errors = []
+    if document.get("openapi") != "3.0.3":
+        errors.append("openapi must be 3.0.3.")
+    info = document.get("info")
+    if not isinstance(info, dict):
+        errors.append("info must be an object.")
+    elif not isinstance(info.get("title"), str) or not info["title"].strip():
+        errors.append("info.title is required.")
+    elif not isinstance(info.get("version"), str) or not info["version"].strip():
+        errors.append("info.version is required.")
+    paths = document.get("paths")
+    if not isinstance(paths, dict):
+        errors.append("paths must be an object.")
+    else:
+        for path, path_item in paths.items():
+            if not isinstance(path_item, dict):
+                errors.append("paths.{} must be an object.".format(path))
+                continue
+            for method, operation in path_item.items():
+                if method.lower() not in {"get", "put", "post", "delete", "options", "head", "patch", "trace", "parameters", "$ref", "summary", "description", "servers"}:
+                    errors.append("paths.{} has unsupported path-item key '{}'.".format(path, method))
+                    continue
+                if method.lower() in {"get", "put", "post", "delete", "options", "head", "patch", "trace"} and not isinstance(operation, dict):
+                    errors.append("paths.{}.{} must be an object.".format(path, method))
+                elif method.lower() in {"get", "put", "post", "delete", "options", "head", "patch", "trace"} and not isinstance(operation.get("responses"), dict):
+                    errors.append("paths.{}.{} must define responses.".format(path, method))
+    _validate_refs(document, errors)
+    return errors
+
+
+def _validate_refs(node: Any, errors: List[str], location: str = "") -> None:
+    if isinstance(node, dict):
+        ref = node.get("$ref")
+        if isinstance(ref, str) and ref.startswith("#/"):
+            target = node_root = None
+            # Local references are resolved from the document root by the caller below.
+            root = getattr(_validate_refs, "_root", {})
+            target = root
+            for segment in ref[2:].split("/"):
+                segment = segment.replace("~1", "/").replace("~0", "~")
+                if not isinstance(target, dict) or segment not in target:
+                    target = None
+                    break
+                target = target[segment]
+            if target is None:
+                errors.append("Unresolved local $ref '{}' at {}.".format(ref, location or "/"))
+        elif isinstance(ref, str) and not ref.startswith("#/"):
+            errors.append("External $ref '{}' is not supported; references must stay within this file.".format(ref))
+        for key, value in node.items():
+            _validate_refs(value, errors, "{}.{}".format(location, key))
+    elif isinstance(node, list):
+        for index, value in enumerate(node):
+            _validate_refs(value, errors, "{}[{}]".format(location, index))
+
+
+def validate_with_refs(document: Dict[str, Any]) -> List[str]:
+    _validate_refs._root = document
+    try:
+        return validate_document(document)
+    finally:

+    version = info.get("version") if isinstance(info, dict) else None

+    return media.get("schema") if isinstance(media, dict) else None

+def _resolve(root, schema):
+    if not isinstance(schema, dict) or "$ref" not in schema:
+        return schema or {}
+    ref = schema["$ref"]
+    if not ref.startswith("#/"):
+        return schema
+    target = root
+    for part in ref[2:].split("/"):
+        part = part.replace("~1", "/").replace("~0", "~")
+        target = target.get(part) if isinstance(target, dict) else None
+        if target is None:

+    resolved.update({key: value for key, value in schema.items() if key != "$ref"})

+    if key in {"minimum", "minLength"}:
+        return new is not None and (old is None or new > old)
+    if key in {"maximum", "maxLength"}:
+        return new is not None and (old is None or new < old)
+    if key in {"format", "pattern"}:
+        return new != old
+    if key == "nullable":
+        return old is True and new is False

+def _normalize_path(path):

+    if finding["direction"] == "request":

+    if not path:

+def _field_matches(changed, used):
+    def normalize(value):
+        return value.replace("[]", "[*]").strip(".")
+    changed, used = normalize(changed), normalize(used)
+    if changed == used:

+    return changed.startswith(used + ".") or used.startswith(changed + ".") or changed.startswith(used + "[*]") or used.startswith(changed + "[*]")

+def _join_path(parent, child):
+    if not parent:
+        return child
+    if child == "[]":
+        return parent + "[]"
+    return parent + "." + child

+

+    if not isinstance(schema, dict):
+        return schema

+# Contract Guard
+
+Contract Guard compares OpenAPI specification versions, shows changes and impact on registered consumers, and applies a publishing gate before a proposed version can be published.
+
+## Run the application
+
+Requirements: Docker with Compose, or Python 3.9+ and Node.js 20+ for local development.
+
+From the project root:
+
+```sh
+docker compose up --build
+```
+
+Open the React application at <http://localhost:5173> and the FastAPI/OpenAPI docs at <http://localhost:8000/docs>. PostgreSQL data is persisted in a Compose volume. Stop with `docker compose down` (data remains in the volume; `docker compose down -v` removes it).
+
+To run services locally without containers, start PostgreSQL and set `DATABASE_URL`, then:
+
+```sh
+python3 -m venv .venv
+. .venv/bin/activate
+pip install -r backend/requirements.txt
+uvicorn app.main:app --app-dir backend --reload
+```
+
+In another terminal:
+
+```sh
+cd frontend
+npm install
+npm run dev
+```
+
+SQLite is used by default if `DATABASE_URL` is not set (convenient for local/test runs). The API reads starter-kit data from `../contract-guard-starter-kit` by default; set `STARTER_KIT_PATH` to override.
+
+## Use
+
+1. Choose **Import starter kit** to register the three providers, four consumer declarations, and all 12 supplied spec files.
+2. Select a provider and choose exact baseline and proposed records. Duplicate imported Claims `1.1.0` versions remain distinct by filename and can be selected explicitly.
+3. Review findings and declared consumer impact. Uploading a regular spec requires YAML/JSON with a valid OpenAPI 3.0.3 document and resolvable local `$ref`s. Duplicate provider/version uploads are rejected; records are never overwritten.
+4. Publish a proposed version against the selected baseline. A blocked attempt is recorded in publish history.
+
+Impact is based only on registered consumer declarations. A “no declared consumer affected” result does not imply there are no other consumers.
+
+## API endpoints
+
+- `GET /api/health`
+- `GET /api/services`, `POST /api/services`
+- `GET /api/services/{service_id}/versions`, `POST /api/services/{service_id}/versions`
+- `POST /api/import/starter-kit`, `GET /api/import/runs`
+- `GET /api/versions/{from_id}/compare/{to_id}`
+- `POST /api/versions/{version_id}/publish?baseline_id={baseline_id}`
+- `GET /api/publish-attempts`, `GET /api/metrics`
+
+The interactive API reference is available at `/docs`.
+
+## Tests
+
+Backend tests:
+
+```sh
+python3 -m venv .venv
+. .venv/bin/activate
+pip install -r backend/requirements.txt pytest
+pytest -q backend/tests
+```
+
+Frontend production build:
+
+```sh
+cd frontend
+npm install
+npm run build
+```
+
+## Current scope and limitations
+
+- Implemented: service registry, starter-kit import, YAML/JSON/OpenAPI structural and local-ref validation, duplicate-version handling, semantic comparison for common OpenAPI schemas/parameters/responses, declared consumer impact, provisional configurable publish policy, publish-attempt history, metrics, and a React UI.
+- Imported invalid specs remain visible with errors so import can complete; invalid user uploads are rejected.
+- The provisional policy blocks breaking changes affecting declared consumers and blocks expired `x-sunset` elements when still used by a declared consumer. Deprecation/sunset policy is centralized in `backend/app/policy.py` and should be updated to match product-owner guidance.
+- No auth/approval workflow, external `$ref` loading, notifications, or CI integration is included yet. Unsupported OpenAPI constructs and classifier edge cases need further coverage before production use.
+- Severity/classification is a heuristic and should be treated as review guidance, not proof of runtime behavior.
+
+## Buildathon documents
+
+- `PLAN.md` — Gate 1 plan
+- `PROGRESS.md` — milestone status
+- `DECISIONS.md` — assumptions and decisions
+- `REVIEW.md` — final self-review (complete before final submission)

1: # Contract Guard
2: 
3: Contract Guard compares OpenAPI specification versions, shows changes and impact on registered consumers, and applies a publishing gate before a proposed version can be published.
4: 
5: ## Run the application
6: 
7: Requirements: Docker with Compose, or Python 3.9+ and Node.js 20+ for local development.
8: 
9: From the project root:
10: 
11: ```sh
12: docker compose up --build
13: ```
14: 
15: Open the React application at <http://localhost:5173> and the FastAPI/OpenAPI docs at <http://localhost:8000/docs>. PostgreSQL data is persisted in a Compose volume. Stop with `docker compose down` (data remains in the volume; `docker compose down -v` removes it).
16: 
17: To run services locally without containers, start PostgreSQL and set `DATABASE_URL`, then:
18: 
19: ```sh
20: python3 -m venv .venv
21: . .venv/bin/activate
22: pip install -r backend/requirements.txt
23: uvicorn app.main:app --app-dir backend --reload
24: ```
25: 
26: In another terminal:
27: 
28: ```sh
29: cd frontend
30: npm install
31: npm run dev
32: ```
33: 
34: SQLite is used by default if `DATABASE_URL` is not set (convenient for local/test runs). The API reads starter-kit data from `../contract-guard-starter-kit` by default; set `STARTER_KIT_PATH` to override.
35: 
36: ## Use
37: 
38: 1. Choose **Import starter kit** to register the three providers, four consumer declarations, and all 12 supplied spec files.
39: 2. Select a provider and choose exact baseline and proposed records. Duplicate imported Claims `1.1.0` versions remain distinct by filename and can be selected explicitly.
40: 3. Review findings and declared consumer impact. Uploading a regular spec requires YAML/JSON with a valid OpenAPI 3.0.3 document and resolvable local `$ref`s. Duplicate provider/version uploads are rejected; records are never overwritten.
41: 4. Publish a proposed version against the selected baseline. A blocked attempt is recorded in publish history.
42: 
43: Impact is based only on registered consumer declarations. A “no declared consumer affected” result does not imply there are no other consumers.
44: 
45: ## API endpoints
46: 
47: - `GET /api/health`
48: - `GET /api/services`, `POST /api/services`
49: - `GET /api/services/{service_id}/versions`, `POST /api/services/{service_id}/versions`
50: - `POST /api/import/starter-kit`, `GET /api/import/runs`
51: - `GET /api/versions/{from_id}/compare/{to_id}`
52: - `POST /api/versions/{version_id}/publish?baseline_id={baseline_id}`
53: - `GET /api/publish-attempts`, `GET /api/metrics`
54: 
55: The interactive API reference is available at `/docs`.

66: ```

72: npm install
73: npm run build
74: ```

76: ## Current scope and limitations
77: 
78: - Implemented: service registry, starter-kit import, YAML/JSON/OpenAPI structural and local-ref validation, duplicate-version handling, semantic comparison for common OpenAPI schemas/parameters/responses, declared consumer impact, provisional configurable publish policy, publish-attempt history, metrics, and a React UI.

+# Self-review
+
+## What works
+
+- The app imports the supplied provider specs and consumer declarations without modifying the starter kit. Duplicate imported version strings remain separate records, and invalid imports are reported without preventing the rest of the import.

+

+
+- Start Docker Compose and exercise the full UI against PostgreSQL.
+- Review policy semantics and supported change classifications with the product owner.
+- Add stricter OpenAPI edge-case tests and API/UI acceptance tests, then improve accessibility and error recovery.
*** End Patch

1: # Contract Guard — Build Plan
2: 
3: ## Problem and users
4: 
5: Contract Guard helps API-owning engineers understand and prevent changes that break known consumers before publishing. Consumer engineers need clear impact and reasons; platform leads need visibility into publishing outcomes. Impact is limited to registered consumer declarations, so reports must say “no declared consumer affected” rather than claim there are no consumers.
6: 
7: ## Requirements and decisions
8: 
9: - Register services/owners; accept OpenAPI YAML/JSON through UI and API; reject invalid uploads clearly.
10: - Compare semantic API behavior, including `$ref`-backed schemas; classify operations, parameters, nested/list fields, types, requiredness, enums, and response code changes.
11: - Register consumer usage; show affected declared consumers and explain findings; block publishing when a declared consumer breaks.
12: - Keep changelog, publish-attempt history, UI, metrics, and one-command startup.
13: - Treat `x-internal` as internal-use metadata and `x-sunset` as end-of-life metadata; extensions are optional.
14: - Provisional policy: block breaking changes only when declared consumers are affected; warn for deprecated/sunset elements before expiry and block after expiry if a declared consumer still uses the element. Keep policy configurable.
15: - Import all supplied specs and consumers without modifying the starter kit. Imported duplicate `info.version` records are preserved and warned about; new uploads colliding on provider + version are rejected without overwriting.
16: - Defer optional webhooks, CI integration, and AI-generated migration help.
17: - Product-owner answers on severity and sunset policy are pending; provisional policy can be adjusted.
18: 
19: ## Research
20: 
21: - oasdiff documents distinct diff, changelog, breaking-change, and validation functions: https://github.com/oasdiff/oasdiff
22: - Apigee API hub documents OpenAPI linting with default/custom rules: https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/apihub/validate-spec
23: 
24: ## Design
25: 
26: - Modular FastAPI backend, React frontend, PostgreSQL persistence.
27: - Modules: registry/import, validation, comparison, consumer impact, publish policy, history/metrics.
28: - Data: Service; SpecVersion with internal ID, `info.version`, source filename, source document and validation status; ConsumerUsage; ChangeFinding; PublishAttempt.
29: - Spec records use internal IDs, not version strings, as identity. Preserve duplicate imported versions distinguished by filename; uploads reject collisions. Never overwrite published history.
30: - UI: services; service/version detail and upload; semantic compare; impact and publish; history and metrics.
31: - API outline: `/api/services`, `/api/services/{id}/versions`, `/api/import/starter-kit`, `/api/versions/{from}/compare/{to}`, `/api/versions/{id}/publish`, `/api/publish-attempts`, `/api/metrics`.
32: 
33: ## Tests and success measures
34: 
35: - Unit: parse/validate, `$ref` handling, version collisions, semantic diff, impact matching, and publish policy including sunset boundaries.
36: - Integration: import/upload/compare/publish persistence; duplicate import retained; upload collision does not overwrite.
37: - Acceptance: import provided kit, verify invalid Claims `$ref`, known consumer impacts, publishing decisions and history.
38: - Metrics: attempts by outcome, breaking changes blocked for declared consumers, affected declared consumers, expired-used elements blocked, invalid specs, collisions detected without overwrite.
39: - Test outcomes will be reported only after tests are executed.
40: 
41: ## Milestones
42: 
43: 1. Registry/import API, persistence, OpenAPI validation, collision behavior.
44: 2. Semantic diff and plain-language change findings.
45: 3. Consumer impact matching and configurable publishing policy/history.
46: 4. React UI, metrics, integration/acceptance tests, and runnable documentation.
